questions.knowledge_point: Integrals Representing Surface Areas Generated by Functions of Y
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14094971/assets/ac4ac44291d75fa4cc75f3b3b4b0a0328d29f08a2a774d603f51a64594d6f8ad.png)

Consider the arc of the curve $x={y}^{3}-6{y}^{2}+9y$ that lies in the first quadrant between its $y$-intercepts. What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $y$-axis by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{3}-6{y}^{2}+9y & =0 \\ y({y}^{2}-6y+9) & =0 \\ y(y-3)^{2} & =0 \\ y & =0,3\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=3.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{3}-6{y}^{2}+9y)=3{y}^{2}-12y+9.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}y\sqrt{1+{(3{y}^{2}-12y+9)}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}y\sqrt{1+9({y}^{2}-4y+3)^{2}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the arc of the curve $y={x}^{3}$ that lies between the lines $x=0$ and $x=\frac{1}{\sqrt[4]{3}}.$ Calculate the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${x}_{1}=0$ to ${x}_{2}=1.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3})=3{x}^{2}\,⇒\,{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}=9{x}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1/\sqrt[4]{3}}{x}^{3}\sqrt{1+9{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the substitution 

$$
u=1+9{x}^{4}\,⇒\,\text{d}u=36{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x,
$$

we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1/\sqrt[4]{3}}{x}^{3}\sqrt{1+9{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{4}\sqrt{u}(\frac{1}{36}\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{18}{\int }_{1}^{4}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{18}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{\sqrt{{u}^{3}}\,|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{27}(8-1) \\  & =\frac{7\pi }{27}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the arc of the curve $x={y}^{2}-{y}^{4}$ that lies in the first quadrant between its $y$-intercepts. What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $y$-axis by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-{y}^{4} & =0 \\ {y}^{2}(1-{y}^{2}) & =0 \\ y & =0,\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=1.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{2}-{y}^{4})=2y-4{y}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y\sqrt{1+{(2y-4{y}^{3})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y\sqrt{1+4{y}^{2}-16{y}^{4}+16{y}^{6}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the arc of the curve $y=\frac{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}{2}$ that lies between the lines $x=0$ and $x=\operatorname{ln}⁡2.$ Calculate the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${x}_{1}=0$ to ${x}_{2}=\operatorname{ln}⁡2.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}{2})=\frac{{e}^{x}-{e}^{-x}}{2}\,⇒\,{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}=\frac{{({e}^{x}-{e}^{-x})}^{2}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(\frac{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}{2})\sqrt{1+\frac{{({e}^{x}-{e}^{-x})}^{2}}{4}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(\frac{{e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}}{2})\sqrt{\frac{4+{e}^{2x}-2+{e}^{-2x}}{4}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}({e}^{x}+{e}^{-x})\sqrt{{e}^{2x}+2+{e}^{-2x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}({e}^{x}+{e}^{-x})\sqrt{{({e}^{x}+{e}^{-x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{({e}^{x}+{e}^{-x})}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}({e}^{2x}+2+{e}^{-2x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}{[\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2x}+2x-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-2x}]}_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}(\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2})-\frac{\pi }{2}(\frac{1}{2}{e}^{0}+2(0)-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-0}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}(\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4+2\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{4}) \\  & =\pi (1+\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\frac{1}{16}) \\  & =\frac{(15+16\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\pi }{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${y}_{1}=0$ to ${y}_{2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{1-{y}^{2}}))=\frac{2y}{1-{y}^{2}}\,⇒\,{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}=\frac{4{y}^{2}}{(1-{y}^{2})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1/\sqrt{2}}y\sqrt{1+\frac{4{y}^{2}}{(1-{y}^{2})^{2}}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1/\sqrt{2}}y\sqrt{\frac{(1+{y}^{2})^{2}}{(1-{y}^{2})^{2}}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1/\sqrt{2}}y\cdot \frac{1+{y}^{2}}{1-{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the substitution 

$$
u=1-{y}^{2}\,⇒\,-\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u=y\,\text{d}y,
$$

we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1/\sqrt{2}}y\cdot \frac{1+{y}^{2}}{1-{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{1/2}\frac{2-u}{u}\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}u \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1/2}^{1}(\frac{2}{u}-1)\,\text{d}u \\  & =\pi (2\operatorname{ln}⁡u-u)\,{|}_{1/2}^{1} \\  & =\pi ((0-1)-(2\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2})-\frac{1}{2})) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}(4\operatorname{ln}⁡2-1) \\  & =\frac{\pi (4\operatorname{ln}⁡2-1)}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
